title: Five Lessons for School Reformers: 2026 Edition
author: Frederick Hess
source: Education Next / Old School with Rick Hess
summary: Frederick Hess, drawing on 35 years of observation from high school teacher to AEI fellow, warns the new generation of school reformers—energized by science-of-reading mandates, school choice expansion, and post-pandemic reckoning—not to repeat the mistakes of the Bush-Obama era. He identifies five lessons: don't mistake legislative wins for lasting victories (the real work follows), resist drinking the Kool-Aid (true believers dismiss legitimate criticism), listen with genuine purpose rather than performing engagement, treat money as a mixed blessing rather than a solution, and recognize that six-sevenths of reform is invisible to outsiders. Written with candor about past failures—Reading First, teacher evaluation, Common Core—he argues that 'reform done poorly is often worse than no reform at all' and that today's reformers face the additional challenge of polarized echo chambers and algorithm-driven social media that make escape from tribal thinking harder than ever.
points: Treat every legislative win as an opening act rather than a destination: the 'implementation problem' in education is not a problem, it is the actual work—budgets and mandates only open doors.
Build feedback loops that surface criticism from outside your circle of trust; echo chambers and algorithm-driven social media make this discipline harder and more important than in past reform eras.
Practice listening as a tool for understanding legitimate concerns and developing solutions, not as a performative step before repeating your talking points more loudly.
Evaluate school reform success by demonstrated student outcomes rather than impressive declarations; given today's information abundance, it is easy to mistake good marketing for substantive change.
Recognize that new funding without changed incentives and practices often provides cover to avoid reform rather than enabling it, and paints a target on the program for critics.
quotes: Reform done poorly is often worse than no reform at all.
The stuff that gets termed 'implementation' is the actual work of reform. Legislative wins, no matter how tough, are just an opening act.

What might that look like in 2026? Well, those who've imbibed too much innovation Kool-Aid might be prone to dismiss ed tech backlash as AI panic, rather than a legitimate response to screen-saturated classrooms and schools' history of fumbling technology.
I'm not close enough to see what's really happening in any given state or school system. Way back when, I was mostly just relating who I liked, who was getting good buzz, and who had good PR.

There's recently been a lot of healthy talk about the importance of 'implementation.' That's good, as long as it's accompanied by an understanding that in education, there's no such thing as an 'implementation problem.'
